The contract traded between 10,878.5 and 10,899.5, compared with Monday’s settlement of 10,883.5. The cash FTSE 100 closed Monday 37.76 points higher at 10,854.32.
Bitcoin provided the strongest overnight move, climbing 4.7% to around US$80,700 after reaching US$81,104 - its highest level since May. It has gained approximately 25% over the past week.
Gold eased 0.3% to around $4,640 an ounce but remained on course for its strongest monthly advance since September 1999, having gained approximately 14% during August. Copper slipped 0.2% to $6.59 per pound.
Australia outperformed, with the ASX 200 rising 0.7% to 9,163. WiseTech Global gained 4.1% to A$45.28 and BHP added 0.6% to A$67.51. Woodside Energy fell 0.9% to A$33.17.
Elsewhere, Japan’s Nikkei 225 advanced 0.4% to around 65,800, South Korea’s Kospi gained 0.5% to approximately 6,730 and the Shanghai Composite added 0.2% to 3,890. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 0.2% to around 25,468.
Wall Street finished mixed. The S&P 500 fell 0.28% and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.76%, while the Dow Jones gained 0.26%. Nvidia dropped 2.91% ahead of its quarterly results on Wednesday.
Brent crude held near US$92.10 a barrel, down 0.1%, following the latest US sanctions against Iran.
summary: London stock indices advanced broadly, with the FTSE 250 outperforming the FTSE 100 as oil prices fell below $90 a barrel. Brent crude slid around 3% after Washington's sanctions on Iran proved less severe than anticipated. Meanwhile, individual corporate performers like Vistry and Melrose posted significant gains following funding awards and positive operational updates.
key_points: The FTSE 250 climbed 0.6% while the FTSE 100 added 0.2% in trading.
Brent crude tumbled roughly 3% to around $89.36 a barrel amid eased supply concerns over Iran sanctions.
Vistry shares jumped up to 16% following a £350 million government funding award for affordable housing.
Melrose led the FTSE 100 with a rise of about 9% after positive updates regarding its GKN Aerospace subsidiary.
Bitcoin surpassed $80,000 for the first time in three months amid bond market intervention discussions.

title: New study shows shock difference in caffeine levels between High Street coffee shops
author: Anna Wise
content:
Those enjoying their morning coffee on the commute face ‘wildly’ different levels of caffeine, a new study shows.
It found people who drink coffee will be taking in more or less caffeine in their drinks than they anticipated, depending on which chain they went to.
The latest research from consumer champion Which? analyses the caffeine content in drinks sold by chains Caffe Nero, Costa Coffee, Greggs, Pret A Manger and Starbucks.
Which? said its research showed customers should “pay attention” to the differences in caffeine levels across high street retailers, particularly for those who are advised to restrict their intake for health reasons, including pregnancy.
It found that a medium cappuccino from Costa contains 325 milligrams (mg) – almost three-and-a-half times as much as the same drink at Starbucks, at 89mg.
The caffeine content in Costa’s cappuccino is the equivalent of around four cans of Red Bull, Which? found.
The second and third-highest cappuccino caffeine levels were found at Greggs and Caffe Nero, at 235mg and 221mg respectively.
Costa also comes out on top for drinks including its espresso shot, which contains 100mg of caffeine per serving, and its flat white, which has 241mg.
In contrast, Starbucks has 45g of caffeine per serving in its espresso shot, and 89mg in its flat white.
While Costa’s caffeine content for cappuccinos and single-shot espressos has not changed since Which?’s last study in 2023, Caffe Nero’s has noticeably increased – which its cappuccino now containing around double the level of caffeine than before.
And while Starbucks continue to serve the least caffeine overall across its drinks, its caffeine levels have increased in its espressos, cappuccinos and filter coffees over three years.
![iced matcha lattes](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/04/15/15/AdobeStock_263152031-2c4d9454.jpeg)
Matcha drinks also vary significantly between the chains – with the drink, made from green tea powder, booming in popularity in recent years and prompting high street coffee chains to put their own versions on the menu.
The study found that Costa’s hot matcha latte contained the highest caffeine content at 99mg, followed by Starbucks at 57mg and Pret at 28mg.
Jessica Carson, Which? health and wellbeing expert, said: “For many of us, there is nothing quite like a strong cup of coffee to start the day, but Which? found even matcha enthusiasts could be consuming more caffeine than intended.
“Our research shows caffeine content varies wildly from chain to chain.
“If you drink multiple cups a day or need to cut back for health reasons, pay attention to where you shop and what you order to avoid any unwanted side-effects.”
A spokeswoman for Costa said: “At Costa Coffee, we’re committed to helping customers make informed choices.
“That’s why caffeine and nutritional information is available across our menu and online, so customers can choose the drinks that best-suit their individual preferences and needs.
“We also offer decaffeinated coffee and a range of non-caffeinated drinks.
“Coffee naturally contains caffeine and levels can vary depending on factors such as the blend, recipe and serving size.”
Starbucks has been contacted for comment.
summary: A new study by Which? reveals wild variations in caffeine levels across major UK high street coffee chains, impacting consumers who need to monitor their intake. Costa Coffee was found to have the highest caffeine levels in drinks like cappuccinos and espressos, while Starbucks consistently recorded the lowest. The research also highlighted significant differences in caffeine content among popular matcha lattes offered by the chains.
key_points: A medium cappuccino from Costa contains 325mg of caffeine, which is nearly three-and-a-half times the 89mg found in the same drink at Starbucks.
Costa also recorded the highest caffeine levels for espresso shots (100mg) and flat whites (241mg).
Caffè Nero's cappuccino caffeine content has doubled since a previous study conducted in 2023.
For matcha lattes, Costa contained the highest caffeine at 99mg, followed by Starbucks at 57mg and Pret at 28mg.
Consumers, especially those restricting intake for health reasons or pregnancy, are advised to pay attention to chain-specific caffeine differences.

title: Gold price hits three-month high amid fears over Iran war and Trump economy
author: Joanna Partridge
content:
Gold prices hit their highest level in more than three months on Tuesday as continued conflict in the Middle East and ongoing political uncertainty fuelled the latest rally in the precious metal.
Gold is viewed as a safe haven by investors and its price tends to rise at times of uncertainty.
The metal has risen by about 15% so far during August, reaching $4,651 (£3,410) an ounce during Asian trading hours on Tuesday, before falling back slightly. This put gold on track for its best monthly performance in almost 30 years, since September 1999.
The price of gold began to rise in early August amid optimism that the US and Iran were getting closer to restoring a ceasefire in the Middle East and reopening the strait of Hormuz. While this did not happen, the price of gold has continued to climb.
The latest rises came as investors awaited US inflation data and a closely watched speech from the new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, amid anxiety in government bond markets over inflation and Donald Trump’s tax and spending plans.
“Looking ahead, we expect dips in gold to be well-supported from buyers looking for gold to make its way towards the next upside resistance at $4,900/$5,000,” said Tony Sycamore, a market analyst at the broker IG.
The price of bitcoin climbed above $80,000 (£58,680) on Tuesday, taking the cryptocurrency to a three-month high not seen since mid-May, which analysts attributed to a weakening US dollar and similar factors that were driving gold higher.
The biggest rally in gold since the 1970s began in 2025, after Trump first announced the introduction of tariffs on imported goods, prompting fears of disruption to global trade.
The price topped $4,000 an ounce for the first time last October, before passing $5,000 in January and reaching a record high at the end of that month, partly fuelled by shifts in US policy, as well as political uncertainty elsewhere, including in France and Japan.
However, many investors were surprised to see the price fall back again earlier this year, reaching $3,942 in late June, despite the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
after newsletter promotion
War and geopolitical uncertainty would usually raise the gold price, making the fall counterintuitive. However, analysts said the US-Iran conflict has also driven oil prices higher, along with expectations of higher inflation and interest rate rises, which are factors that can subdue the gold price, outweighing demand for it as a safe store of wealth.
There is renewed appetite for gold among investors as a “hedge against unclear US fiscal plans”, as a “hedge against inflation, amid questions over the Fed’s willingness, or ability, to fight inflation independently” and as a hedge against worries about the AI boom, according to Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at the Swiss banking group Swissquote.
It comes as Trump has announced fresh tariffs on cars and crucial raw materials from Canada, marking the latest deterioration in relations between the two neighbours, while the US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran.
summary: Gold prices reached a three-month high on Tuesday, driven by ongoing Middle East conflicts and political uncertainty, putting the metal on track for its best monthly performance since September 1999. Investors are increasingly viewing gold as a safe haven and a hedge against inflation, unclear US fiscal plans, and worries about the AI boom. Additionally, bitcoin prices climbed above $80,000 on the same day, influenced by a weakening US dollar and similar market factors.
key_points: Gold prices rose to $4,651 an ounce during Asian trading hours on Tuesday.
The metal has surged by about 15% during August, marking its best monthly performance in nearly 30 years.
Bitcoin prices also climbed to a three-month high above $80,000 due to a weakening US dollar and similar market drivers.
Investors are utilizing gold as a hedge against inflation, unclear US fiscal plans, and geopolitical uncertainty.

title: Lego sales rise as World Cup and F1 ranges prove to be winners
author: Sarah Butler
content:
Lego sales have risen by more than a fifth as tie-ups with the football World Cup, Formula One and the hit film KPop Demon Hunters as well as its flower-based and Star Wars kits drive demand.
The Danish toymaker said its revenues had increased by 21% to 41.9bn Danish kroner (£4.8bn) in the first six months of 2026, driven by strong growth in the Americas, Europe and the Asia Pacific regions. Sales by its clients to consumers rose by 22%.
Net profit increased 32% to 8.6bn Danish kroner (£1bn) as the group launched 330 new products including its hi-tech Smart Play kit, with bricks that emit sounds and light.
Niels B Christiansen, the chief executive of Lego Group, said: “We are very pleased with our strong start to 2026 and the excitement we see for the Lego brand. Our portfolio of products offers something for everyone, and culturally relevant brand experiences continue to drive demand across the globe. Our success in the market means we can maintain high investment levels in growth and sustainability for both the short and long term.”
He said Lego was expanding solar energy capacity at all of its factories. In June, it began constructing its largest solar installation so far in Billund, Denmark – its main headquarters and the home of the original Legoland park. The site, which will begin operating next year, will feature 160,000 panels able to produce 99 GWh a year. It is designed to match the company’s electricity needs in the town.
Lego also said it was also continuing its global shift towards using paper bags in its packaging and expected that to be completed next year.
The company has led a resurgence in the toy market in the past year, as adults look for an alternative entertainment to phones and TV screens.
“Kidults” (buyers aged 12 and over) are spending spare cash on expensive Lego sets and collectible figurines. This group is behind £1 in every £3 spent on toys in the UK, and these buyers spent 10% more in 2025 than the year before according to a study by the market research company Circana.
after newsletter promotion
With toys linked to a wide range of interests, from sports such as Formula One to hit films and TV shows including KPop Demon Hunters and Stranger Things, the British Toy and Hobby Association has said there appears to be an “evolving era of play, where toys are increasingly embedded in wider cultural moments, enjoyed by all the family”.
summary: Lego reported a 21% increase in revenue to 41.9bn Danish kroner for the first half of 2026, driven by popular tie-ups with the World Cup, Formula One, and films like KPop Demon Hunters. Net profit rose 32% to 8.6bn kroner, supported by strong demand globally and growth among adult consumers. The company is also investing in sustainability, including expanding solar energy capacity at its factories and transitioning to paper packaging.
key_points: Revenues increased by 21% to 41.9bn Danish kroner in the first six months of 2026.
Net profit grew by 32% to reach 8.6bn Danish kroner.
Sales were boosted by new products and cultural tie-ups including Formula One, the World Cup, and KPop Demon Hunters.
Lego is expanding solar energy capacity, including a large installation in Billund, Denmark.
Demand is increasingly driven by 'kidults' (buyers aged 12 and over) seeking alternatives to screens.

title: Aldi resorts to ‘whinging’ as rivals steal a march
author: Tom Haynes
content:
![Illustration](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499447186_17875931250250_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Illustration](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499447186_17875931250250_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
With its cheap prices and no-frills stores, Aldi has repeatedly disrupted the status quo of the big four supermarkets over the past decade. But now there are signs that the German discounter is running out of steam.
Giles Hurley, the chief executive of Aldi UK, went on the warpath last week by attacking supermarket loyalty schemes for offering a “false sense of value”.
The outburst went down like a lead balloon in the industry, with some saying Aldi’s criticism of rival supermarkets was designed to deflect attention from its flagging growth.
That has raised questions over whether Aldi can maintain its early promise as a retail juggernaut – or be beaten at its own game by a resurgent Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons.
Hurley was accused by retail leaders of being “desperate” after his attack on loyalty schemes.
Aldi was “completely talking their own book”, one senior retail adviser said by wading into the row over supermarket pricing, which is under investigation by the UK competition watchdog.
“It was opportunistic, and in a way, perhaps a little bit desperate,” they said.
The timing is awkward for Aldi. Its sales rose by just 0.8pc in the 12 weeks to Aug 8, according to NIQ – compared with 8.2pc at Lidl, 13pc at M&S, 17pc at Ocado and 3.6pc at Sainsbury’s.
Aldi has continued opening new shops, making the slowdown more significant.
Clive Black, from Shore Capital, said the discounter was “protesting a bit too much”.
“The fact that [customers are] choosing to shop more at other retailers tells us something about Aldi, and it’s not just about price,” he said.
Hurley is responsible for putting Aldi on the map in Britain.
Having joined the retailer nearly 30 years ago, the Irishman took the top job in 2018 and oversaw the opening of its 1,000th store in 2023.
He took aim at his own industry last week, writing a piece for the Daily Mail backing the Government’s investigation into supermarket pricing.
Hurley said shoppers were being bombarded with discounts that could make them believe they are getting a bargain – when a rival supermarket is still cheaper.
“Taking £2 off a £6 product doesn’t make it good value if you can buy it for £3 somewhere else,” he said.
The attack piece made sense for Aldi. The company does not operate a loyalty scheme like Tesco’s Clubcard or Sainsbury’s Nectar Prices.
Its argument is that shoppers should get its lowest prices without having to sign up, hand over their data or use a smartphone.
But for some, the move belied a desperate bid to once again steal a march on Britain’s established supermarkets as they became increasingly adept at copying Aldi’s strategy.
Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons are among those advertising “Aldi price match” products.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Britain’s competition watchdog, has examined loyalty pricing, looking at around 50,000 grocery products.
It found very little evidence that supermarkets were artificially inflating prices before applying discounts.
Loyalty card members could “almost always” make a genuine saving against the normal price, although some loyalty deals remained more expensive than the cheapest option elsewhere.
Black was equally dismissive of Aldi’s argument that shoppers were being duped.
“British shoppers are not stupid,” he said, pointing out that Tesco and Sainsbury’s now compete with Aldi on hundreds of high-volume products.
“You can see that they’re growing more slowly than the big four – more slowly than Lidl,” he added.
Aldi’s complaints also come at a significant moment for the discounters more broadly.
The CMA has proposed extending rules governing supermarket land agreements to Aldi and Lidl, arguing that their size and geographic reach mean they should now be treated like the established chains.
Until now, the discounters have had greater freedom to use restrictive agreements that can prevent rivals opening stores nearby.
“I think they’re really feeling it, and the CMA ruling is a big thing for them actually, because until now they’ve had a lot of freedom,” Black said. “It’s a very significant moment in the development of the discounters here. It does have the potential to change the dynamics of the market.”
Aldi’s push to offer shoppers the cheapest prices – earlier this year it cut the prices of potatoes, carrots and parsnips to 4p – is also under renewed scrutiny.
Britain’s farmers are already under pressure from rising labour and input costs and increasingly unpredictable weather. There are fears Aldi’s cut-price approach is helping kill off British agriculture by offering unrealistic prices to shoppers.
The Government’s Farming Profitability Review warned that farm input costs are expected to be 30pc higher this year than in 2020, and called for farmers to receive “a fair return for what they produce”.
Black believes supermarkets cannot endlessly compete to make food cheaper without eventually putting pressure on the people producing it.
“To be devaluing fresh produce ... giving a packet of carrots away for 8p when it costs £4.50 for a cup of coffee is just not helpful to the sustenance of the food system,” he said.
“We need a food system from farm to fork that is financially sustainable. And I think that does involve paying more for food.”
Aldi rejects any suggestion that its low prices come at the expense of British farmers.
It says it has committed £5bn to British farming and food production through longer-term agreements covering fruit, vegetables, dairy, meat and eggs.
It has also committed £3bn to British beef suppliers over five years and £1.1bn to British egg production.
Aldi says its model is based on efficiency rather than squeezing suppliers.
“Loyalty programmes are expensive to run and ultimately lead to higher prices,” an Aldi spokesman said.
“We fundamentally believe that the best way to keep grocery bills low for customers is to keep things simple.”
For Aldi, however, simplicity is becoming harder to sell as its rivals adopt its methods.
Black said the retailer should stop attacking its rivals.
“When we saw Aldi effectively trying to badmouth competitors in a way that was encouraging politicians to get involved, I thought that was bad form,” he said.
Aldi changed the way Britons shop, but it now risks becoming part of the status quo it once set out to smash.
summary: Aldi UK chief executive Giles Hurley recently criticized rival supermarkets' loyalty schemes for offering a false sense of value, prompting accusations of desperation from industry leaders as the discounter experiences slower sales growth than competitors like Lidl. The public attack coincides with a UK competition watchdog investigation into supermarket pricing and proposed rule changes that would strip discounters of certain freedoms regarding land agreements. Meanwhile, Aldi's ultra-low pricing strategy on fresh produce has drawn scrutiny from experts over its potential impact on the financial sustainability of British farmers.
key_points: Aldi UK CEO Giles Hurley attacked rival supermarket loyalty schemes, claiming they offer a false sense of value to shoppers.
Industry leaders accused Aldi of being desperate and using the criticism to deflect attention from its slower sales growth compared to rivals like Lidl.
Sales at Aldi rose by just 0.8pc in the 12 weeks to August 8, lagging significantly behind competitors such as Lidl, M&S, Ocado, and Sainsbury's.
The Competition and Markets Authority has proposed extending rules on supermarket land agreements to include Aldi and Lidl, ending some of their regulatory freedoms.
Aldi defends its pricing model as being based on efficiency rather than supplier pressure, highlighting multi-billion-pound commitments to British farming and food production.

title: Your morning coffee could be four times stronger than a Red Bull
author: Susanna Galton
content:
Dr Duane Mellor is an honorary associate professor at the University of Leicester and a registered dietitian and science communicator. The findings, he says, demonstrate just how difficult it can be for consumers to judge their caffeine intake simply by the drink they order.
Why does the caffeine content vary?
Mellor says some of this could be explained by the beans used. Arabica beans are naturally lower in caffeine than Robusta, which he says can contain up to twice as much caffeine per bean.
“Robusta has a much bigger yield, so it is cheaper, and it can possibly deal with weather changes a bit more,” he says, adding that Robusta beans are also more bitter.
The amount of caffeine can also rise considerably with the size and number of shots in a drink. Which? found that a large Costa cappuccino contains four espresso shots, while a small flat white contains three.
Customers who want to reduce their caffeine intake can ask for fewer espresso shots, while those who drink several takeaway coffees a day may want to pay attention to where they are buying them, as well as what they order.
What this means for your health
Mellor says body size, genetics and how regularly somebody consumes caffeine can all influence its effect. People with anxiety or who experience heart palpitations may want to be particularly cautious, as caffeine can temporarily raise blood pressure. However, it’s worth remembering that moderate coffee drinking is associated with lower cardiovascular risk.
A big caffeine hit may be more noticeable than the same amount spread across the day. Regular coffee drinkers can also become accustomed to caffeine, and reducing it suddenly can cause symptoms such as headaches.
Some people also experience a “caffeine crash”, which can happen four to six hours after drinking caffeine. Signs of a caffeine crash include headaches, excessive tiredness, an inability to concentrate and irritability.
For most of us, accidentally consuming more caffeine in one or two drinks might do no more harm than leaving us feeling more jittery. Mellor says the main concern is in pregnancy, as too much caffeine can lead to complications. “For expectant mothers, the recommended upper limit is 200mg of caffeine a day,” he says. “This means that with some of the coffees tested, you could easily exceed that with one cup.”
The timing matters too. “If you drink caffeine later, you may get more sleep disturbances,” Mellor says. “Having it a good four to six hours before sleeping is recommended.”
Should you opt for decaf?
Not necessarily, particularly if you enjoy coffee and don’t experience adverse effects from caffeine.
Moderate coffee consumption has been associated in observational research with a lower risk of conditions including cardiovascular disease, type two diabetes and dementia. But Mellor stresses that it isn’t clear that caffeine is responsible. “Whether that’s linked to the caffeine is unclear,” he says. “You sometimes see in studies that decaffeinated coffee can have the same effect.”
summary: Caffeine content in coffee varies significantly based on bean types, serving sizes, and the number of espresso shots, sometimes resulting in levels much higher than energy drinks. While moderate coffee consumption can be associated with health benefits, high caffeine intake poses risks for pregnant women and can cause side effects like increased blood pressure, sleep disturbances, and caffeine crashes. Consumers can manage their intake by paying attention to what they order and requesting fewer espresso shots.
key_points: Robusta beans contain up to twice as much caffeine per bean compared to Arabica beans.
Drink size and the number of espresso shots, such as four shots in a large Costa cappuccino, drastically increase caffeine levels.
Excessive caffeine intake is a primary concern during pregnancy, where the recommended limit is 200mg per day.
High or late caffeine consumption can lead to sleep disturbances, temporary blood pressure spikes, and caffeine crashes.
Moderate coffee drinking is linked to lower risks of cardiovascular disease, type two diabetes, and dementia, though decaf may have similar effects.

title: Why is cracking clay causing train troubles?
author: Jodie Halford
content:
![Train tracks stretch off into the distance. The rails go off as far as the eye can see, and small stones and rocks surround the railway sleepers underneath.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/a353/live/12e8dae0-9fc5-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Train operators say the long, hot summer and lack of rain has led to issues with track quality in some areas
- Published
A summer of record-breaking temperatures is drawing to a close - with the prolonged heat and lack of rainfall having taken its toll on the land beneath us.
Rail bosses say the clay that sits under the railway in Essex has dried out and shrunk because of the weather, leading to issues with the quality of the track.
Earlier this month, a train derailed in Lewes, Sussex, injuring 30 people, followed by another derailment in Wickford just over 24 hours later.
What are rail companies doing to make sure trains and tracks are safe? And how are they trying to protect train travel against climate change?
Why is cracking clay a problem?
![A pair of hands holds a pile of dirt which is broken up into small pieces](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/069c/live/642b0d00-9fc6-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
July 2026 was the driest in England since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office
Described by the British Geological Survey (BGS) as "one of the most damaging geohazards in the UK today", changes to clay can affect buildings and infrastructure such as railways.
Soil in some areas contains clay minerals which absorb water and swell when wet, then lose water and shrink as it dries out.
This can lead to problems with whatever's been built on top, for example train tracks becoming uneven.
Last year, Network Rail said it wouldn't be safe to run trains at full speed, external if the track moved - and that areas between Salisbury and Exeter were particularly vulnerable to clay changes, along with Essex.
It also said peat soil north of Ely in Cambridgeshire behaved in a similar way to clay after prolonged periods of hot and dry weather.
"The Victorians didn't know much about the makeup of the soil when they built much of our railway in the 1800s," Network Rail said.
"Engineers then didn't know how the railway would react in the dry summers we're experiencing, which they couldn't have predicted back then."
Slower speeds and timetable changes
![A graphic of a train track with part of the track highlighted by a white box with "Track irregularity seen prior to the incident" written above it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/594c/live/63f98d20-9bde-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Investigators found a defect on tracks in Lewes, East Sussex at the site where a train derailed leaving 30 injured
GBR Anglia - which involves train operators Greater Anglia and c2c, as well as track operator Network Rail Anglia - says safety is its top priority, and it's having to make some changes as a result of what's happened to the ground this summer.
Passengers will notice timetable changes on the c2c route from 25 August and on the Greater Anglia line between Southend Victoria and London on Tuesday 1 September.
You might notice slower speeds once you're on board, too - some journeys will take between two and eight minutes longer than usual, and will have slightly amended departure and arrival times.
On Monday, c2c said it "strongly recommends" customers travelled earlier in the day or after peak times where possible, and told passengers to expect short notice delays and cancellations until further notice.
If you regularly catch a certain service, it's worth checking for the latest before you travel on c2c or Greater Anglia's websites.
How long will this go on?
![A small group of people in orange hi-vis clothing and white hard hats stand on train tracks in front of a train that is slightly leaning to one side near a railway crossing bridge](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/077d/live/abe56fb0-9fc5-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Just one day after the train derailed in Lewes, there was another derailment in Wickford, Essex - no-one was injured
At the moment, it's not clear how long the ground will take to recover.
GBR Anglia says until it's done so, the speed restrictions will need to be kept in place.
It also says its engineers are "closely monitoring track conditions across the region" and there's a chance they'll have to bring further speed restrictions in over the next few weeks to keep services running smoothly.
Network Rail previously said once moisture returned to the ground, processes to repair and smooth out the tracks - more on that below - would be much longer lasting and trains could return to normal speeds.
Will this keep happening every year?
![A large, bright yellow machine is on train tracks in the dark. It is lit by lights on the machine and people operating it are wearing hi-vis orange clothing and white hard hats.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b001/live/d2435dc0-9fc5-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
GBR Anglia says tamping machines help create a solid foundation underneath tracks using ballast
Scientists have found that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change in the future.
Network Rail says it's spending Â£2.6 billion on track maintenance and renewals, and has started a programme to protect the railway from extreme weather and climate change.
It's laying on extra engineering work, using machines called tampers to help create a solid foundation underneath tracks.
It's also putting in new ballast, the stones underneath the rails and sleepers, to help raise the level of track.
In 2025, engineers used tampers to treat 100km (62 miles) of track affected by dried-out soil in the Essex area.
They also dropped thousands of tonnes of ballast to smooth out the tracks this summer, and said 49,000 tonnes were expected to be dropped across 2026.
Dickon Ross, editor of Rail Magazine, says tampers and ballast are a "temporary fix", and that he expects to "see some recurrence of these issues".
"The measures they're taking aren't long term, but they've got to be done," he told the BBC.
"In the longer run, I think technology can be used for predictive maintenance - as well as helping to avoid failures, it'll pinpoint what needs fixing and help with efficiency and safety."
Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.
summary: Record-breaking summer temperatures and a lack of rainfall have dried out and shrunk clay soil beneath railway tracks in areas like Essex, causing uneven tracks and recent train derailments. To ensure safety, rail companies have implemented slower speeds, timetable adjustments, and service delays. Engineers are using temporary fixes such as tamping machines and adding ballast stones, while Network Rail works on long-term weather protection programmes.
key_points: Prolonged hot and dry weather has caused clay soil beneath railways to dry out and shrink, leading to uneven tracks and quality issues.
Recent train derailments occurred in Lewes, Sussex, injuring 30 people, and in Wickford, Essex, 24 hours later.
Train operators have introduced speed restrictions, timetable changes, and journey delays across affected routes for safety reasons.
Engineers are applying temporary fixes like adding ballast stones and using tampers to create a solid foundation under the tracks.

title: Burnham ‘shelves Thames Water administration plan’
author: Pui-Guan Man
content:
Andy Burnham has shelved plans to place Thames Water into emergency administration amid fears over soaring costs, according to reports.
The Government had been preparing for a special administration regime (SAR), a type of nationalisation, for the debt-laden water company.
However, officials recently raised concerns about the cost of a possible administration to the taxpayer, as well as the prospect of legal challenges from rival bidders for Thames Water.
The Government is now working on whether there is a viable alternative for putting the utility into administration, with a decision unlikely for several months, according to The Times.
However, the prospect of Mr Burnham putting the group into administration is looking increasingly slim, the report said.
The Treasury could face a bill of about £2bn if Thames Water enters a SAR, reflecting the funding the company says it needs to remain operational until the end of next year.
Any administration would allow the firm, which supplies about 16 million customers across London and southern England, to continue providing essential services while a long-term buyer was found.
Mr Burnham has been a fierce critic of Thames Water and has previously said it should be nationalised.
He has also frequently promised to bring Britain’s utilities under greater public control.
Mr Burnham’s about-turn is likely to be welcomed by Thames Water’s creditors, who have been scrambling to secure control of the utility with a proposed £10bn restructuring.
The company has been struggling under a £20bn debt pile and risks running out of cash as soon as October.
On Monday, its lenders lined up four new board directors as part of a potential clear-out of its existing leadership.
The proposed new board would include Mike McTighe, the Openreach chairman, Liz Barber, the former Yorkshire Water chief executive, Clive Selley, the former Openreach chief executive, and Dame Bernadette Kelly, a former permanent secretary at the Department for Transport.
Under a 10-year turnaround plan, the new investors said they would take no dividends for a decade or until Thames Water returns to the stock market with a London listing.
Thames Water’s ageing network has also been under renewed pressure from one of the driest summers on record.
It has been battling more than 1,000 leaks every week as the clay soil in the ground dries out and causes pipes to crack.
The Government has been contacted for comment.
summary: Andy Burnham has reportedly shelved plans to place the debt-laden Thames Water into emergency administration due to concerns over high costs to taxpayers and potential legal challenges from rival bidders. The debt-laden utility, which is struggling under a £20bn debt pile, faces the risk of running out of cash by October. Meanwhile, creditors are pursuing a proposed £10bn restructuring plan that includes appointing four new board directors.
key_points: Andy Burnham has shelved plans for a special administration regime for Thames Water due to soaring costs and legal challenges.
Placing the company into administration could cost taxpayers about £2bn to keep it operational until the end of next year.
Thames Water is struggling under a £20bn debt pile and risks running out of cash as soon as October.
Creditors are attempting a £10bn restructuring plan which includes lining up four new board directors.

title: FTSE 100 Live: London marks positive start to last week of August
author: Ephrem Joseph; Jamie Ashcroft
content:
FTSE 100 Live: London marks positive start to last week of August
Last updated: 16:01 24 Aug 2026 BST, First published: 07:05 24 Aug 2026 BST
- FTSE 100 adds 46 points to trade near 10,862
- Wall Street mixed at open
- Airtel Africa and Weir Group lead blue-chip risers
- IAG, InterContinental Hotels and industrial miners advance
- Healthcare, technology trusts and BP weigh
- FTSE 250 edges into negative territory
4:00 pm: FTSE holds steady gains as quiet August afternoon draws toward close
London's blue-chip benchmark was printed 46 points higher, at 10,862 with just over a half hour of trading left in what has frankly been a gentle start to the last full trading week for August.
With Nvidia's results coming later in the week, and the market's off-peak season coming to a close sooner, its safe to say we'll be seeing more action in the near future.
3:20 pm: Mixed bag after Wall Street open
Wall Street opened the week mixed, with the Dow up 0.2% at 53,382 while technology stocks dragged on the broader market. The S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,643 and the Nasdaq dropped 1% to 25,926 as investors weighed geopolitical developments, major tech earnings and fresh economic signals.
Oil prices eased ahead of further detail on an expected US sanctions announcement, with Brent and WTI down roughly 1.5% to 2% at around $91 and $85 a barrel respectively. The 10-year Treasury yield also edged lower to about 4.71%, offering some relief after last week’s sharp rise in longer-dated yields.
Alibaba was among the notable tech fallers after pricing a HK$80 billion, or US$10.2 billion, equity placement to fund further investment in artificial intelligence. The shares were down about 1.4% after the open, with investors otherwise largely in a holding pattern ahead of the week’s bigger market catalysts.
1:20 pm: Wall Street set for soft start
Wall Street was set for a softer start to the week after US-Canada trade talks broke down over the weekend, with Dow futures down 0.1%, S&P 500 futures off 0.2% and Nasdaq futures falling 0.6%. Washington imposed new tariffs on Canadian goods, prompting Prime Minister Mark Carney to suspend negotiations and pledge like-for-like retaliation.
Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve’s Jackson Hole gathering, with bond yields and the interest-rate outlook firmly in focus. Swissquote senior analyst Ipek Ozkardeskaya cautioned that “US yields won’t magically fall” while government debt grows and Middle East tensions keep energy prices elevated. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is also expected to outline a fiscal consolidation plan this week.
Nvidia headlines a busy earnings calendar, with options markets pricing a roughly 4% move in either direction following its results. Salesforce, CrowdStrike, Intuit and Workday are also due to report, leaving technology stocks at the centre of a week shaped by trade tensions, bond-market nerves and Fed policy signals.
12.30 pm: Miners and travel shares keep FTSE 100 higher
The FTSE 100 remained modestly higher around midday trade, adding 13 points, or 0.1%, to 10,830 after reaching a session high of 10,846.
Market breadth was positive, with 63% of blue-chip constituents trading higher at noon.
Airtel Africa led the index with a 2.6% rise, followed by Weir Group at 2.1%. Anglo American gained 1.8% and Antofagasta advanced 1.6% as copper prices strengthened.
Travel shares also performed well. InterContinental Hotels and International Airlines Group both climbed approximately 1.8%, while Whitbread gained 1.2%.
The advance extended across several sectors, with Halma, WPP, Diageo, Diploma and Rolls-Royce all rising by more than 1%.
Fresnillo headed the fallers with a 1.9% decline despite gold remaining higher. Rightmove and Polar Capital Technology Trust lost 1.5%, while AstraZeneca, Auto Trader, GSK and BP fell by more than 1%.
The FTSE 250 slipped 0.1% to 24,703. ME Group led the mid-cap risers, while Kainos and Hochschild Mining were among the largest fallers. The FTSE Small Cap was flat and the AIM All-Share added 0.1%.
11.30 am: Oil pares losses as Iran threatens ships; BP and Harbour fall
Oil prices recovered from their morning lows as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz intensified, although both major benchmarks remained lower for the session.
Front-month Brent traded around $93.10 a barrel, down 1.4% from Friday’s $94.39 settlement but above its $92.05 intraday low. West Texas Intermediate was 2.3% lower at approximately $85.10 after touching $84.69.
The recovery followed reports that Iran had threatened 46 ships with fines, detention or confiscation for allegedly breaching its new navigation rules. The vessels include ships operated by Abu Dhabi’s Adnoc and South Korea’s Sinokor.
Washington is due to unveil further sanctions against Iran at 6pm BST, potentially targeting countries and companies that continue trading with Tehran. Iran has threatened to halt Gulf oil exports if other countries support the US campaign.
FTSE oil and gas shares showed a mixed response:
- BP fell 1% to 543.9p from Friday’s 549.5p close.
- Harbour Energy dropped 1.5% to 258.2p from 262p.
- Shell eased 0.3% to 3,401p from 3,409.5p.
- Ithaca Energy was broadly unchanged at 273.2p, against 273p previously.
10.15 am: Mining and industrial shares lift London
The FTSE 100 strengthened by 22 points, or 0.2%, to 10,838 as gains among miners, financial companies and industrial stocks outweighed weakness in energy and pharmaceuticals.
Endeavour Mining climbed 5.3%, while Antofagasta gained 2%, Anglo American advanced 1.5% and Rio Tinto added 0.4%. Fresnillo bucked the trend, falling 1.6%.
Industrial stocks were also firm, led by Halma, Weir, Diploma and Rolls-Royce, which gained between 1.3% and 1.7%.
Banks and insurers added support. Standard Chartered rose 1%, Aviva and Hiscox gained around 1.1%, while Barclays, Lloyds and NatWest advanced approximately 0.6%.
Lower oil prices weighed on BP and Shell, down 1.2% and 0.3%, respectively. AstraZeneca fell 0.8% and GSK lost 0.5%.
The broader London market was marginally positive. The FTSE 250 added 0.06% to 24,734, the FTSE SmallCap was flat at 8,202 and the AIM All-Share rose 0.09% to 812.71.
9.20: Miners rise but broader London market remains subdued
The FTSE 100 remained virtually flat after its opening hour, declining around 4 points, or 0.04%, to 10,813.
The subdued tone extended across the main London indices. The FTSE 250 fell 0.12% to 24,689, while the FTSE 350 and FTSE All-Share both declined 0.05%. The AIM All-Share edged 0.05% higher.
Airtel Africa led the blue-chip risers with a 2.3% gain. Copper miners were also stronger, with Antofagasta up 1.5% and Anglo American gaining 1.2%. Diageo rose 1.4% and 3i Group added 1.1%.
Kingfisher headed the fallers, declining 1.1%. Auto Trader, BAE Systems, AstraZeneca and Melrose Industries were all approximately 1% lower.
On AIM, Tracsis (AIM:TRCS) jumped 7% to 342.5p after reporting full-year trading in line with expectations and completing its £48 million acquisition of FirstGroup’s Mistral Data business. FirstGroup recovered after falling around 7% during the opening exchanges.
Spot gold remained 0.8% higher at approximately US$4,640 an ounce, while copper futures were broadly unchanged at US$6.59 per pound. Bitcoin traded near US$77,300, down 0.6%.
Oil remained lower as investors awaited details of the new US sanctions against Iran, due to be announced later today.
8.15am: FTSE opens flat as AstraZeneca weighs
The FTSE 100 opened at 10,818.25 before easing 6 points, or 0.06%, to 10,810. The index traded between 10,802.50 and 10,822 during the opening minutes. Live FTSE data
Airtel Africa led the early risers with a 1.2% gain, followed by Halma at 1.1% and Hiscox at 0.9%. Antofagasta added 0.8%, Entain rose 0.7% and Glencore gained 0.3%.
AstraZeneca was the main blue-chip drag, falling around 1%. Informa and Melrose declined approximately 0.7%, while Sage slipped 0.5%.
FirstGroup provided the morning’s most notable move. Its shares fell as much as 7% to 166.9p before recovering to 179.2p, leaving them just 0.1% lower
Spot gold remained firm at around US$4,646 an ounce, up 0.95%, while copper was broadly flat at US$6.59 per pound.
Brent crude traded near US$93.16, down around 1.3%, ahead of the United States unveiling additional sanctions against Iran. BP opened lower, while Shell was broadly unchanged.
Asian markets were mostly weaker, with South Korea’s Kospi down 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng around 1.8% lower and Japan’s Nikkei off 0.7%. The ASX 200 bucked the trend with a 0.5% gain.
7.30 am: London faces cautious start
The FTSE 100 is expected to open only slightly higher on Monday as investors assess fresh US pressure on Iran, elevated bond yields and mixed commodity prices.
London’s blue-chip index finished Friday 0.6% higher at 10,816.56, supported by miners and other resource stocks.
Gold rose 0.8% to around US$4,645 an ounce, supported by a softer dollar and safe-haven demand. Copper eased to US$6.58, down 0.04% per pound, potentially producing a mixed opening for London-listed miners.
Brent crude dropped around 1.5% to US$93 a barrel ahead of new US economic measures targeting Iran. Lower oil prices may weigh on BP and Shell while providing some relief for airlines, retailers and other energy-intensive companies.
Markets remain alert to possible Iranian retaliation affecting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has warned neighbouring countries against supporting Washington’s latest campaign.
Asian markets were mostly lower on Monday. South Korea’s Kospi sank 3.5% as Samsung plunged following a shareholder-return plan that disappointed investors.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 2.1%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 and Taiwan’s Taiex lost 0.5%. The Shanghai Composite declined 0.7%. Associated Press.
Alibaba shares fell sharply in Hong Kong on HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) equity placement to finance further investment in artificial intelligence.
Australia bucked the regional trend, with the S&P/ASX 200 finishing 0.5% higher near 9,107. Miners led the advance as BHP gained around 3.4% and the materials index reached a record high.
Ansell surged around 18% following its annual results, while Data#3 and uranium producers Paladin Energy and Deep Yellow gained more than 10%. Nib Holdings, Endeavour Group and Aussie Broadband were among the leading fallers. Market Index
Bitcoin traded near US$77,100, while US equity futures edged lower. With the UK economic and corporate calendars relatively quiet, geopolitics, commodities and bond yields are likely to determine London’s early direction.
summary: London's FTSE 100 marked a positive start to the final full trading week of August, adding 46 points to trade near 10,862. Gains were largely driven by mining, industrial, and travel shares, which helped offset declines in energy and pharmaceutical stocks. Meanwhile, global markets navigated fluctuating oil prices, upcoming US tech earnings, and geopolitical tensions.
key_points: The FTSE 100 closed up 46 points at 10,862, led by risers such as Airtel Africa, Weir Group, and various industrial miners.
Oil prices eased ahead of anticipated US sanctions on Iran and amid tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, weighing on energy companies like BP.
Wall Street opened mixed with technology stocks dragging on the broader market as investors awaited Nvidia's upcoming earnings.
US-Canada trade talks broke down over the weekend, resulting in Washington imposing new tariffs and prompting a suspension of negotiations by Canada.

title: Lime pulls bikes from London borough after blind man's 'very frightening' road ordeal
author: Nicholas Cecil; Luke Reevey
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after poorly parked cycles force blind man into busy road](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/9/29/Beal.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Jason Beal, 53, stressed that his Labrador Retriever guide dog Caine baulks at leading him into the road in south east London.
So, unable to see traffic as it goes by, he has to listen out and “very nervously” take Caine into the carriageway with him.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/11/22/Beal1.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Assistive technology manager Mr Beal and his wife Jessica, 45, who is also blind, raised the dangers they were facing with their local MP Liam Conlon.
Lime had been operating in Bromley without a contract with the council which has told it to remove its bikes immediately.
Speaking to The Standard, Mr Beal said: “There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement.
“Then I’ve got to stop, Kent House Road is quite a busy road.
“He (Caine) will refuse to go into a road at any time.
“So, I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road.
“That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”
He added: “Alternatively, there have been times when we have been walking up to the station and there have been loads of bikes parked up against where the tactile pavement is and I’ve had to go into the edge of the road there.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/13/30/lime1.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Marketing audience manager Mrs Beal, 45, who walks using a white cane, told how she has injured herself colliding with e-bikes: “You never know when they are going to crop up and if you are going to hit one, or are they going to fall on you.
“So, it’s quite scary just walking around.”
The couple recognise that “bikes are a great way for people to get around” but stressed it “feels unfair” that they were being left in their way in “difficult places for us”.
Mrs Beal described as “fantastic news” that Lime was removing its bikes from their neighbourhood.
“It does feel like a victory although obviously we want people to continue riding bikes and walking,” she added.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/11/08/blindman.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Conlon, Labour MP for Beckenham and Penge, told of his “real anger” over the ordeal faced by the Beals.
Read More
“We cannot allow new barriers to be created for disabled residents who already face challenges getting around,” he said.
“As a disabled person myself, who was unable to walk for four years as a teenager, I understand these issues first-hand.
“It is something I take seriously, and something I will not accept.”
He added: “I’m delighted that Lime have announced they are withdrawing their bikes from Penge – and would like to thank them for their cooperation, and for their apology.”
It is understood that the Lime app allowed bikes to be hired in the Penge area last week but by Monday morning this was no longer possible.
In a letter to Mr Conlon, Lime stressed the benefits of the e-bikes but also that it is “critical” that their use “works for both riders and the communities in which they operate”.
The company added: “We would therefore like to apologise to Jessica and Jason for the issues they have faced due to rider parking in Penge.
“To address the specific issue in Penge...we have made a change to the Lime app to prevent Lime bikes from being used beyond the Lewisham boundary until we can agree an approach that supports the roll-out of an effective local scheme, with appropriate parking locations.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/11/26/Liam2.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Lime had been operating its bikes in Bromley on a “non-contractual” basis.
It emphasised that the “build-up of bikes” at the border with Lewisham showed a “considerable demand” for rental bikes in Bromley.
It is keen to work with the council and Mr Conlon on a scheme that “works for your constituents, ensuring both appropriate parking solutions for residents to access the service and the removal of bikes parked irresponsibly”.
Councillor Simon Fawthrop, Bromley council’s executive councillor for transport and highways, said, “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough, with their map allowing hiring use in Penge in the last few weeks.
“We welcome it appears to have changed now.
“This remains a serious matter and needs to permanently stop and ultimately if it does not, we will take action to remove the Lime bikes and then charge Lime for these costs.”
summary: Lime has withdrawn its e-bikes from the London borough of Bromley following complaints from a blind couple who were forced into busy roads by poorly parked cycles. Jason and Jessica Beal raised the issue with local MP Liam Conlon after experiencing dangerous obstructions on pavements and tactile paving. In response, Lime apologized and updated its app to prevent bikes from being used beyond the Lewisham boundary until an agreed local scheme with proper parking is established.
key_points: Poorly parked Lime bikes forced a blind man with a guide dog and his blind wife into a busy road in south east London.
Lime was operating in Bromley without a contract or council consent, prompting the council to demand the bikes be removed.
Local MP Liam Conlon intervened on behalf of the couple, expressing anger over the barriers faced by disabled residents.
Lime apologized to the couple and updated its app to stop bike usage beyond the Lewisham boundary.

title: New weight loss pill on sale in UK raises regulation concerns
author: Sophie Braybrook
content:
A new daily weight loss pill, also designed to treat diabetes, is now on sale in pharmacies and online across the UK.
The tablets, made by the US pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly, have already been approved for private sale while discussions are going on with the medical spending watchdog NICE, which could make them available on the health service.
Pharmacists say it will make the treatment much easier for people who can’t tolerate injections.
There are warnings, though, of a lack of rigour in the way the drugs can be obtained without an in-person consultation.
summary: A new daily weight loss and diabetes pill manufactured by Eli Lilly is now available for private sale in UK pharmacies and online. While pharmacists highlight its benefit for patients who cannot tolerate injections, the rollout has raised regulatory concerns regarding the lack of in-person consultations. Meanwhile, discussions continue with NICE regarding potential availability on the National Health Service.
key_points: Eli Lilly's new daily weight loss and diabetes pill is currently on sale privately in UK pharmacies and online.
The medication is being discussed with NICE to potentially make it available on the health service.
Pharmacists note the pill offers an alternative for individuals unable to tolerate injections.
Critics have raised concerns over the lack of rigour in obtaining the drug without an in-person consultation.

title: Energy complaints soar as households brace for higher bills
author: Christopher Jasper
content:
![woman preparing roast dinner](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499359591_17875112679050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5R01ldk3PMF1QsJ9Q8epUWLsxPjsv_nCViLv6rPaIZU.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![woman preparing roast dinner](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499359591_17875112679050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5R01ldk3PMF1QsJ9Q8epUWLsxPjsv_nCViLv6rPaIZU.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Customer complaints about energy suppliers have soared as rising bills pile pressure on households.
The Energy Ombudsman said it accepted 46,532 new cases through June, an increase of 16pc from a year ago. It marks the first half-year rise in complaints since 2023 when Britain was in the grips of an energy crisis following the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Billing disputes accounted for three in every five claims, the Ombudsman said, while complaints about smart meters made up 10pc.
It comes as Ofgem is expected to announce an increase in the October energy price cap on Wednesday.
Analysts at research group Cornwall Insight have forecast that average annual energy bills will rise by 4pc to £1,729 from Oct 1, the highest level in three years.
That would represent a £66 increase for a typical household, wiping out savings from Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on energy, which is projected to deliver an annual saving worth £43.
Separate forecasts by the energy supplier EDF predicted a similar rise to £1,722 in October, and a further increase to £1,815 in January.
The latest increase has been driven by the war in Iran, which has cut global oil and gas supplies and left European gas storage operators struggling to refill stocks before winter.
Bills are set to jump just as demand for heating begins to climb, despite Labour’s manifesto pledge to bring down energy costs by £300.
While much of the escalation has resulted from the Iran war, analysts have warned that the cost of delivering net zero and a decarbonised grid by 2030 is also pushing up bills.
Complaints to the Energy Ombudsman have increased for three straight quarters.
Ed Dodman, the chief ombudsman, said: “The findings in this report highlight the continued challenges facing many energy consumers at a time of ongoing pressure on household finances.
“We will continue to monitor complaint trends closely and work with suppliers to address areas of concern and ensure consumers can access fair, timely resolutions when things go wrong.”
The Energy Ombudsman said there had been some positive developments, with complaints about customer service down 5pc to 3,500 in the half-year. More firms are also meeting their obligation to inform customers of their right to refer disputes to the ombudsman’s office.
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in June it would bolster the office’s powers and improve access for consumers, including cutting the timeframe for escalating disputes from eight weeks to six and allowing compensation when remedies were delayed.
summary: Customer complaints to the Energy Ombudsman rose by 16pc to 46,532 new cases in the first half of the year as rising energy bills put pressure on households. Billing disputes made up three in five claims, driven by a price cap increase tied to reduced global supplies from the war in Iran and the costs of delivering net zero. Ofgem is expected to announce a higher energy price cap, pushing typical annual bills up to £1,729 from October.
key_points: Energy Ombudsman accepted 46,532 new cases through June, a 16pc year-on-year increase.
Billing disputes accounted for 60pc of all claims, while smart meter complaints made up 10pc.
Cornwall Insight forecasts average annual energy bills will rise by 4pc to £1,729 from October 1.
The upcoming bill increases are driven primarily by the war in Iran and costs associated with the net zero transition.
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero plans to bolster ombudsman powers, including cutting the dispute escalation timeframe to six weeks.

title: Households in Great Britain ‘could owe energy suppliers £7bn by end of year’
author: Jillian Ambrose
content:
Households in Great Britain could owe their energy suppliers as much as £7bn by the end of the year after higher gas and electricity prices forecast for the winter kick in, an industry group is warning.
Domestic energy debt and arrears climbed by about £500m over the past year to a record £6bn at the end of June as the Middle East conflict continued to stoke rising gas market prices.
The amount of energy debt left unpaid for longer than 30 days is likely to accelerate to £7bn by the end of the year, according to the trade association Energy UK, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is expected to climb to a three-year high.
The regulator is expected to confirm later this week a 4% increase on the energy price cap for millions of households from October as “too many households continue to feel the strain of high energy bills”, the group’s chief executive, Dhara Vyas, said.
She urged Andy Burnham’s government last week to consider a “targeted and more permanent” solution to the rise in energy bills – including a social discount tariff – rather than rely on “stopgap, ad hoc or emergency measures”.
The increase will more than wipe out the impact of the new prime minister’s promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from October, which aimed to give voters “some breathing space” by shrinking bills by an average of about £45 a year.
“The current arrangements fail to provide the help needed and work out more costly,” Vyas said. “A social discount will address the fuel poverty gap and provide the right amount of support to the right households at the right time – reflecting that needs vary across different customers.”
  The forecast energy price cap rise means that over the final three months of 2026 the typical household faces a gas and electricity bill equivalent to £1,729 a year, forecasters at Cornwall Insight predict.
The consultancy expects electricity rates to rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.57p, and gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.90p for households that pay via direct debit. However, the actual bill for a household will depend on how much each consumes.
The average bill under the price cap was calculated assuming lower annual energy use than in previous years, because the high cost of energy has forced many households to use less gas and electricity as debt levels rise. Using the previous methodology, the price cap would be forecast to rise to £1,940.69 from October – the highest level since the summer of 2023.
after newsletter promotion
Ahead of the new cap, Energy UK told journalists that the rising cost of sourcing gas from the global wholesale market was the single largest contributing factor to the expected rise, although the expense of upgrading Great Britain’s energy networks was also playing a larger role in setting energy costs.
The trade group’s debt estimates are about £1bn higher than the official figures reported by Ofgem, which counts unpaid bills only once they are 90 days overdue. Although it uses a lower debt figure publicly, it spreads the cost of unpaid bills across all consumers using the higher estimates. This currently adds about £50 a year, or about 3% extra, to a typical annual bill.
summary: Households in Great Britain could owe up to £7bn to energy suppliers by the end of the year as gas and electricity prices are forecast to rise. Domestic energy debt already reached a record £6bn at the end of June due to rising gas market prices driven by the Middle East conflict. Industry group Energy UK warns that upcoming price cap increases will worsen fuel poverty and urges the government to implement a targeted social discount tariff.
key_points: Domestic energy debt and arrears reached a record £6bn at the end of June.
Unpaid energy debt past 30 days is projected to hit £7bn by the end of the year.
The energy price cap is expected to rise by 4% in October for millions of households.
Energy UK recommends a targeted social discount tariff rather than temporary emergency measures.
Rising global wholesale gas costs and network upgrade expenses are driving the expected price increases.

title: Shein closes in on £20bn Hong Kong listing after ditching London
author: Chris Price
content:
![Shein billboard](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499406363_17875587178980_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Shein billboard](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499406363_17875587178980_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Shein will press ahead with a £20bn listing in Hong Kong next month after abandoning plans to go public in London last year.
The fast-fashion giant, which was founded in China but is based in Singapore, aims to raise HK$13.86bn (£1.3bn) on Sept 1.
The online retailer confirmed in a filing that it was looking to sell its stock at around HK49.50 per share, giving the business an overall valuation of about £20bn. That would value Shein well below the £50bn it was seeking just a year ago.
It also suggests its valuation has fallen by 70pc from its peak four years ago after listings in London and New York were scuppered.
The company, which sells cheap dresses and jeans in 160 countries, has been hit with allegations of human rights abuses and faces a crackdown on its business model in the EU and the US.
It had submitted papers for an initial public offering in London in 2024, but long delays in regulatory approval meant it went cold on the plan.
While it did eventually secure the go-ahead from the Financial Conduct Authority for a version of its listing plans, this was rejected by Chinese regulators, in a blow to Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, as she sought to revive the City.
MPs had criticised the lack of transparency around the company’s supply chain. Some raised concerns that it was using cotton from Xinjiang, the Muslim-majority part of China where there have been accusations that the local Uyghur population has been coerced into manual labour.
Shein has previously said it “strictly prohibits forced labour” in its supply chain.
The retailer only won Beijing’s approval for a listing last month to make its public market debut in Hong Kong.
The online retailer plans to offer 280 million shares at a price between HK47.60 and HK49.50.
Its cut-price listing comes after it also faced questions regarding slowing growth, rising costs and changing market conditions.
Investors had said they were not convinced Shein could return to the growth rates that valued it at nearly $100bn (£73bn) four years ago.
In the UK, smaller retailers have accused the Government of allowing the fast-fashion giant to operate on an unfair playing field.
Under current rules, the de minimis threshold allows goods valued at £135 or less to be imported from overseas directly to consumers without customs duty needing to be paid. It was announced in last year’s Budget that the exemption would be phased out in the coming years.
Shein swung to a $99m quarterly loss after the US removed similar import duty exemptions.
summary: Fast-fashion giant Shein is proceeding with a £20bn listing in Hong Kong next month, aiming to raise £1.3bn after abandoning plans for a London IPO. The company's valuation has dropped significantly from past peaks due to regulatory hurdles, human rights allegations regarding its supply chain, and challenges in key Western markets. Additionally, Shein recently reported a quarterly loss following the removal of import duty exemptions in the United States.
key_points: Shein is targeting a £20bn valuation for its Hong Kong listing on September 1, aiming to raise HK$13.86bn (£1.3bn).
The company abandoned its previous plans to go public in London following regulatory delays and objections from Chinese regulators.
Shein's current valuation represents a substantial decline from a peak of nearly $100bn four years ago.
The retailer has faced criticism from MPs and investors over supply chain transparency, human rights allegations, and changing market conditions.
Shein recently posted a quarterly loss after the US removed import duty exemptions that previously benefited low-value direct-to-consumer shipments.

title: Rail service changes in east London and Essex due to dried-out clay
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Rail service changes in east London and Essex due to dried-out clay
There are going to be changes to Greater Anglia and c2c train services from tomorrow (Tues 25th Aug) as the railway deals with the side effects of the recent heatwaves.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/Uneven-track-on-the-c2c-route-caused-by-dried-out-soil-measures-are-in-place-to-keep-services-running-safely-smoothly-and-reliably.jpg)
Because of sustained heat and low rainfall, the clay under long stretches of the railway in Essex has dried out and shrunk, causing track quality issues. To keep everyone moving safely and reliably, speed restrictions and temporary timetable amendments are being applied to give passengers more certainty about services and reduce the risk of short-notice disruption.
Timetable changes will come into effect on the c2c route on Tuesday 25 August and on the Greater Anglia line between Southend Victoria and London on Tuesday 1st September.
GBR Anglia says that some journeys will take 2–8 minutes longer than usual, with slightly adjusted departure and arrival times.
While speed restrictions are currently not affecting Elizabeth line services, customers are advised to check for the most up-to-date travel information before starting their journey.
Engineers are closely monitoring track conditions across the region, and further speed restrictions may be needed in the coming weeks to keep services running smoothly. GBR Anglia says it will advise of any additional service alterations in advance.
Speed restrictions will remain in place until ground conditions recover, which will require a prolonged period of rain.
To minimise the effects of dried-out soil on Anglia this summer, extra engineering work will continue, with Network Rail using machines called tampers to help create a solid foundation so that trains can run smoothly. Engineers are also laying new ballast (the stones underneath the rails and sleepers) to help raise the track level.
Last year, railway engineers used tampers to treat around 100km of track affected by dried-out soil on Anglia. Ahead of this summer season, thousands of tonnes of ballast were dropped to help keep the track as smooth as possible, with 49,000 tonnes expected to be dropped during 2026 in total.
Martin Beable, Chief Operating Officer for GBR Anglia, said: “We’re taking action to keep everyone moving safely and reliably while minimising the impact on passengers. Our teams are working together across Anglia to keep running the best possible service despite the significant challenges we’re facing because of this exceptionally hot and dry weather.
“We never want our customers to experience disruption, but safety will always be our priority. Thank you for bearing with us, and please do check before you travel, particularly if you’re used to getting the same time train every day.”
summary: Recent heatwaves and low rainfall have dried out and shrunk the clay beneath railways in east London and Essex, leading to track quality issues. To maintain safety, Greater Anglia and c2c are introducing speed restrictions and temporary timetable changes starting August 25 and September 1. Journeys may take two to eight minutes longer, and restrictions will remain in place until prolonged rainfall allows ground conditions to recover.
key_points: Sustained heat and low rainfall caused clay beneath the railway in Essex to dry out and shrink.
Speed restrictions and temporary timetables begin on August 25 for c2c and September 1 for the Greater Anglia line.
Affected journeys will take two to eight minutes longer with adjusted departure and arrival times.
Network Rail is using tampers and laying new ballast to help stabilize the tracks.
Speed restrictions will remain in place until a prolonged period of rain allows the ground to recover.

title: New once-daily weight loss pill now available in pharmacies across UK
author: Storm Newton
content:
A new daily pill to manage diabetes and assist with weight loss will be available at pharmacies across the UK from Monday.
Pharmacists said that the rollout is “particularly significant” for patients who are unable to use weight loss jabs.
The drug is called orforglipron and is sold under the brand name Foundayo. It was manufactured by American pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly and was authorised by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) earlier this month.
It is the second GLP-1 pill for weight loss to be made available through UK pharmacies, after Wegovy in July.
The UK is the first country in Europe to approve the pill.
Eli Lilly said that it is working with the NHS spending watchdog, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, on its assessment of Foundayo for a potential rollout on the health service in England.
![The new once-daily weight loss pill called Foundayo is now available in the UK](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/17/9/14/Foundayo-Carton_0-8mg_Lilly-Medicine-Image.jpg)
The medication is licensed for people with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, or people with a BMI between 27 and 30 who have at least one weight-related condition.
It can also improve blood sugars in patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes.
The pill is taken once a day, at any time, with no food or water restrictions.
Dosage begins at 0.8mg, climbing to 2.5mg, 5.5mg, 9mg, 14.5mg, and 17.2mg.
Patients will spend a minimum of one month at each dosage level.
“We’re pleased that this means there is another oral treatment option for eligible UK patients alongside licensed injectable treatments,” Khalil Asmar, vice-president of cardiometabolic health at Lilly Northern Europe, said.
Henry Gregg, the chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association, said that it is “another significant day”.
“This is particularly significant for patients who cannot or do not want to take an injectable medicine and could make weight loss treatment available to a wider range of patients.
“It is easier for criminals to provide fake, unlicensed or counterfeit versions of oral medications than injectables and patients must make sure they only access weight loss treatments through safe and regulated pharmacies.
“There must now be a redoubling of efforts within government and the NHS to use pharmacies to make sure more eligible patients in clinical need can get weight loss treatments on the NHS, rather than the current postcode lottery that exists for weight management services via GPs.”
summary: A new once-daily weight loss and diabetes pill called Foundayo, manufactured by Eli Lilly, is now available in UK pharmacies. The medication is authorized for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher, or a BMI between 27 and 30 with a weight-related condition. It marks the second GLP-1 oral treatment available in the UK and provides an alternative for patients who cannot or prefer not to use weight loss injections.
key_points: The drug is called orforglipron, sold under the brand name Foundayo, and was authorized by the MHRA.
The UK is the first country in Europe to approve the once-daily pill.
Eli Lilly is working with NICE regarding a potential rollout of the drug on the NHS in England.
The medication dosage starts at 0.8mg and can increase up to 17.2mg, with patients spending at least one month at each level.

title: Trains hit with speed restrictions over derailment risk
author: Gareth Corfield
content:
Network Rail has been forced to slow trains amid fears of more derailments.
Trains in southern Essex will run more slowly from Tuesday as a result of clay beneath railway lines having dried out during the ongoing drought.
It comes after two trains, one in Essex, derailed during the hot weather earlier this month.
Speed restrictions and timetable amendments are being imposed on services between London and Southend via both the c2c and Greater Anglia (via Rochford) routes.
Some services will take up to eight minutes longer to reach their destinations than usual, meaning a typical hour-long journey from Shoeburyness, south Essex, to London will be just more than a tenth longer than normal.
Clay shrinks when it dries out, leading to what Network Rail described as “issues with the quality of the track”.
Martin Beable, chief operating officer of Great British Railways Anglia, which runs c2c and Greater Anglia-branded services, said: “Our teams are working together across Anglia to keep running the best possible service despite the significant challenges we’re facing because of this exceptionally hot and dry weather.
“Thank you for bearing with us, and please do check before you travel, particularly if you’re used to getting the same time train every day.”
summary: Network Rail has imposed speed restrictions and timetable changes on train services in southern Essex starting Tuesday due to the risk of derailments. The restrictions are necessary because ongoing drought conditions have caused clay beneath the railway lines to dry out and shrink, compromising track quality. Following two recent derailments during hot weather, affected services between London and Southend may take up to eight minutes longer than usual.
key_points: Speed restrictions affect c2c and Greater Anglia routes between London and Southend.
The measures are a response to clay beneath the tracks drying and shrinking during the drought.
Two trains derailed in hot weather earlier this month, including one in Essex.
Affected journeys will take up to eight minutes longer than normal.

title: John Caudwell and Stuart Rose blast ‘tax creep’
author: Mauricio Alencar
content:
![John Caudwell in a formal setting, possibly during a business meeting or public speaking event, conveying professionalism.](https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/John-Caudwell.jpg?w=742) 
Billionaire political donor John Caudwell and retail bigwig Lord Stuart Rose have hit out at the “creep of taxes” hitting businesses across the country.
The influential business veterans have joined a campaign led by entrepreneur group Helm calling on the government to “stop the creep of taxes on wealth creators”.
A letter, which has been signed by Pimlico Plumbers’ former boss Charlie Mullins and Gail’s Bakery chairman Luke Johnson, urges Labour to stop rolling out new tax hikes on founders, including levies on dividends, capital gains and business assets.
Lord Rose, the former chairman of Asda and Marks & Spencer, said he had “never been more concerned about the cost of doing business” and added that taxes and regulation had become “serious impediments to growth and employment”.
