A squeezy bottle of Venetian-red, perfectly smooth and thick puree. A mousse-like texture and a plain, sweet-forward flavour with that classic sour twang. Sugar is at 21%, and the tomato ratio is on the low side (148g per 100g ketchup). Contains modified maize starch.
Tesco tomato ketchup
![Tesco Tomato Ketchup.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bee9d9cce63f0afb140bef3a3aefd962642c355a/500_0_4000_4000/master/4000.png?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
★★☆☆☆
Sweet on the nose, with a thin consistency and a slimy texture from the modified maize starch. Low in total sugars (17.9%), while 148g tomatoes per 100g sauce is also on the low side.
For more, read the best supermarket mayonnaise and the best supermarket English mustard
summary: Supermarket tomato ketchups were tested and rated, showing that even economical sauces performed well when paired with chips. Tomato content and sugar levels varied across brands, with some products utilizing modified maize starch as a thickener. Rubies in the Rubble Ketchup but Gooder was named best overall, while Bramwells Original tomato ketchup took the best bargain spot.
key_points: Rubies in the Rubble Ketchup but Gooder was rated best overall due to its high fruit content and spiced, fruity depth.
Bramwells Original tomato ketchup won best bargain with its simple, additive-free formula that is well suited for kids.
Tomato content in the tested products varied significantly, measured either by raw weight before cooking or as a straight percentage of puree.
Some ketchups with lower tomato content used modified maize starch as a thickening agent.

title: Revealed: Reform rakes in £20m in donations from crypto investors
author: Harriette Boucher
content:
Nigel Farage’s Reform UK has received £20m in donations from cryptocurrency investors since the general election, The Independent can reveal.
An analysis of Electoral Commission data shows that a staggering 60 per cent of the right-wing eurosceptic group’s funding comes from wealthy individuals associated with the digital currency since the beginning of 2024.
The largest donations, totalling £15m, came from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, whose separate undeclared donation of £5m directly to Mr Farage is the subject of a parliamentary probe.
Other donors include Ben Peter Delo, the founder of cryptocurrency trading platform BitMex, who gave two £2m payments to the party this year and Maria Rost, the wife of US crypto investor John Rost, who has given nine payments worth £125,000.
Simon William Smith, a London-based bitcoin investor who founded a company which allows content creators to sell their content in exchange for Bitcoin, donated £116,000 ahead of the general election in 2024. Oscar Townsley, the founder of Bitcoin derivatives trading firm A1X, gave the party £30,000 last year.
By comparison, the Conservative Party received £82,250 in donations from Alan Eldad Howard, a hedge fund manager and crypto investor. The Independent did not identify any such donations for Labour, Lib Dems or the Green Party.
A Reform UK spokesman said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with all donations.”
![The majority of Reform’s funding is from individuals tied to the crypto sector](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/15/11/farage-crypto-indycomp.jpeg)
The revelations will pile further pressure on Mr Farage, who was re-elected as Clacton MP earlier this month after he dramatically quit in protest at intense scrutiny over Mr Harborne’s £5m donation, which he insists was a personal gift.
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, told The Independent: “Nigel Farage has spent the summer battling a bin in a desperate attempt to dodge scrutiny but people have a right to know what he’s hiding.
“He secretly took a £5m ‘gift’ from a Thai-based crypto billionaire and then promised to cut taxes for the crypto industry.
“Now it seems his party is awash with crypto cash. Farage is treating the public with contempt. With donations from a convicted fraudster and police probes into Reform’s donors and finances – it’s clear they think the rules are for other people."
What are the other parties’ stance on cryptocurrency?
Labour has taken a strict stance on cryptocurrency, with Sir Keir Starmer imposing a temporary ban on cryptocurrency donations and a cap on donations from Britons living abroad to political parties as part of a wider government review into electoral interference. No other parties have promoted pro-crypto policies and the Greens have called for a ban on “unethical” crypto adverts in the London Underground.
![Stella Creasy is seeking an amendment that would cap donations from any individual](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/04/03/18/House-of-Commons_250403_UK-US-Trade-and-Tariffs---Secretary-of-State-for-Business-and-Trade-15_52952.jpg)
Labour MP Stella Creasy wants the government to go further and fears its cap could only create a loophole that people with British postcodes will exploit.
She is fighting for an amendment to cap donations from any individual and prevent everyone from having “an outsized influence on British politics because of the amount of money they can give”.
“I think the public should be worried full stop,” she said. “What I fear is coming is the wholesale distortion of democracy whereby a small number of disproportionately loud voices determine outcomes because of the funding they offer.
“Even if there is no connection between Mr Farage receiving substantial sums of money and his views on cryptocurrencies, the appearance of it undermines our democracy. Just as the appearance that individual donations to my own political party might be shaping outcomes, or to the Conservatives, or to the Greens, or the Lib Dems.”
She added: “But if it walks like a duck and it talks like a duck, you can see why people are squawking.”
Labour MP Catherine West told The Independent: “The late Robin Williams once suggested that politicians should wear jackets with the names of the people who are sponsoring them. In Reform's case, it seems to be a magic cloak that disappears when difficult questions are asked.
“Ordinary people across the country need nothing less than full disclosure on who exactly is trying to buy their way into UK legislation.”
![Nigel Farage claimed his party would make London one of the major crypto trading centres of the world](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/05/29/23/e6c328282f522be10a057aa21bf58c0eY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzQ4NjQwNjYy-2.80399283.jpg)
Experts have warned of the dangers of accepting such large donations from a tiny group of people, saying many will likely be seeking a “return on investment” and may be hoping to influence policy or party stance.
Tory MP Harriet Baldwin, former chair of the Treasury committee, said: “In the US, President Trump has profited personally from liberalising the rules around cryptocurrencies. It would be regrettable if the UK became a place where politicians used power over independent regulators for their own personal enrichment.”
What are Reform’s policies on cryptocurrency?
The £20m received by Reform does not include £614,000 in donations and payments from individuals and groups tied to the sector, declared by Mr Farage. He also has shares in Stack BTC, a UK bitcoin treasury.
Since the general election, he and his party have fought to liberalise the crypto market, argued against state involvement in the sector, and published draft legislation that hopes to ignite a “crypto revolution” in Britain.
It is a stance shared by Farage ally Donald Trump who has championed the digital currency and heavily profited from crypto while in office.
The US president has unveiled several crypto-friendly policies since and made more than $1.4bn (USD) from business dealings in cryptocurrency last year.
During a bitcoin conference in Las Vegas, Mr Farage promised to enact his Cryptoassets and Digital Finance Bill if Reform won at the next general election.
The draft piece of legislation promised to cut taxes on crypto profits and create a Treasury bitcoin reserve fund. It has since disappeared from Reform’s website.
Stuart Wilks-Heeg, a politics professor at the University of Liverpool, said the large proportion of Reform’s funding coming from individuals with crypto ties was “significant”. He said individuals typically donated to parties because they have a shared ideology, want influence, or expect something in return.
He told The Independent: “These are some of the biggest donations in British political history, and it's a sector that a lot of people have concerns about for good reason.
“The easiest party to influence in terms of policy is clearly Reform, because it's not internally democratic. Basically, what Nigel says goes. So if you've got Nigel's ear, you can shape policy.”
![Donald Trump made more than $1.4bn (USD) from business dealings in cryptocurrency last year](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/09/16/27/trump-farage-oval-office.jpeg)
Sam Power, a leading expert in political financing at the University of Bristol, said the donations were essential for a party that has such a shallow funding base.
“We have never in British politics seen a party of that shape and size secure the kind of income that they [Reform] have.
“It’d be hard to look at Reform’s view on crypto and think that crypto donors backing them wouldn’t think they’ve spent their money wisely.”
summary: Nigel Farage's Reform UK has received £20m in donations from cryptocurrency investors, accounting for 60 per cent of the party's funding since the beginning of 2024. Major contributions include £15m from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and £4m from BitMex founder Ben Peter Delo. The substantial funding has drawn scrutiny and criticism from opposing politicians regarding potential policy influence on cryptocurrency regulations.
key_points: Reform UK has taken in £20m in crypto-related donations since the beginning of 2024, making up 60 per cent of its total funding.
Crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne provided the largest share of these donations, totaling £15m.
Other notable crypto donors include BitMex founder Ben Peter Delo, who contributed £4m through two separate payments.
Reform UK states that it follows all Electoral Commission guidelines and practices stringent vetting for its donations.
Politicians and experts have raised concerns that the large donations could be used to buy influence and shape pro-crypto party policies.

title: Stoke-on-Trent bus travel restricted for children under 15
author: Alex McIntyre; Paula White
content:
![A purple and white bus with "7 Kidsgrove" on the screen at the top drives towards us along a road.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/de08/live/30571bc0-9e0b-11f1-95e0-53a570c83624.jpg)
First Bus said children under 15 years old would have to be accompanied by an adult after 18:00
- Published
Children under 15 have been banned from travelling alone on buses in the evening in Stoke-on-Trent to tackle anti-social behaviour, it has been revealed.
First Bus confirmed the youngsters would have to be accompanied by an adult when travelling on services to and from Hanley Bus Station after 18:00.
The restriction, which came into effect on Friday, was approved by the Department for Transport following discussions with Staffordshire Police and the city council, the operator said.
Currently, children aged five to 15 can travel on most bus services in England for free, external as part of a government scheme, which is due to run until the end of August.
The restriction in the Potteries covers 32 services in total and drivers have been told to "exercise their discretion" over whether to allow unaccompanied children onto the bus if there were concerns about their safety.
Rebecca Arrowsmith, general manager of First Bus in the area, said there had been "growing incidents" of anti-social behaviour at the bus station and on board services.
"The safety of our staff and customers is always our number one priority and we will always take steps to ensure everyone on board can travel in comfort and without nuisance," she explained.
"This measure has the full support of the council and will be kept under daily review. We hope to be able to end the restriction as soon as possible."
Simon Mathieson, the firm's regional director for the East and Midlands, said the decision had been made "regrettably".
He said the aim was to remove the restriction once the free bus travel offer came to an end.
"We have seen a large uptake in the area for children using this scheme, which is great," Mathieson told BBC Radio Stoke.
"Buses are important, buses matter. We know people like to travel by bus. Obviously, the weather has been fantastic, with people getting out and about.
"We've seen good use of this scheme, but we just need people to act sensibly when they're on the bus and in the bus station."
summary: Children under 15 are now banned from travelling alone on First Bus services in Stoke-on-Trent after 18:00 to address growing anti-social behaviour. The restriction, affecting 32 services to and from Hanley Bus Station, requires youngsters to be accompanied by an adult. The measure was approved by the Department for Transport and will be kept under daily review until the government's free bus travel scheme for children ends in August.
key_points: Unaccompanied children under 15 cannot travel on Stoke-on-Trent buses after 18:00.
The rule applies to services traveling to and from Hanley Bus Station.
The restriction was implemented to combat rising anti-social behaviour.
Drivers can use their discretion if an unaccompanied child's safety is a concern.
Operators hope to lift the restriction once the national free bus travel scheme ends in August.

title: £700 plug-in solar panels to go on sale in days - where to buy them
author: Adam Forrest
content:
Plug-in solar panel kits are set to go on sale in the UK this Thursday, just in time for Britons to catch the end of the sunny weather.
British company UKSOL, selling its one-panel solar kit for £699, has become the very first to meet regulatory compliance for the devices.
It will be on sale for delivery through Argos and other suppliers on 27 August. But plug-in solar products are not expected to be widely available to buy inside supermarkets or other high-street stores before the end of summer.
There had been expectations that plug-in solar kits would be available for around £400 as part of the Government’s push to get widespread take-off this summer.
But experts said the cost of some plug-in products may be higher than expected – explaining that prices will vary depending on the size and level of power different kits can generate.
There are still hopes that prices will come down in future, if the self-install panels become as popular as they are in Germany and other parts of Europe.
Regulation changes on Thursday
UK households will be permitted to use compliant devices from 27 August after Labour ministers pushed through legal changes last month.
UKSOL was the first company to get their plug-in solar kits listed as compliant by the Energy Networks Association (ENA). Two of its kits – designed for mounting in the garden, rather than on balconies – will be on sale from that date.
Argos and City Plumbers, a builders’ merchants with 350 branches, confirmed the plug-in solar kits will be available for households to buy.
The kits will also be available on UKSOL’s website and from other specialist suppliers. But they will initially be available only for delivery, rather than by picking up in store.
Retailers such as Lidl, Asda, B&Q, Currys, Screwfix and Wickes have all expressed interest in solar kits.
None of the firms has set a specific launch date for the devices but the Government expects some major retailers to have the kits on sale for delivery on 27 August.
However, the expectation is that they will not be available to buy in the supermarkets aisles or inside retail branches for a while, The i Paper understands.
Major outlets are still working out the logistics of stocking large products, so it could take several weeks before any are available in store.
First plug-in kits will reduce energy bills
UKSOL’s 460W single panel system – which comes with a 800W microinverter that allows the panel to start generating power – will sell for around £699. It also comes with a mounting kit and an app to monitor its performance.
The more powerful 890W system will sell for £999. This two-panel system helps to generate more power when sunshine is low in autumn and winter – even though the microinverter will cap the level of electricity at a maximum of 800W.
The prices include VAT but do not include home delivery, which may cost more.
![UKSOL new plug-in solar panel kits comes ready to stand in the garden (Photo: Supplied)](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309029739.jpg?w=644)
“It’s exciting,” said chief executive Andrew Moore. “It’s going to give people a feel-good factor because they’re going to generate some of their own power in an eco-friendly way.
“It’s going to reduce their energy bills, and means less reliance on energy companies,” he added.
The amount of power users can generate has been limited to 800W per electricity circuit by the Government.
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has estimated that plug-in solar users will be able to reduce energy bills by £70 to £110 a year.
“We think that with the bigger kit, if you can generate something close to 800W, the saving could more than that,” said Moore.
“But how much is difficult to say. It depends on where they are placed, if they’re away from shading, how much sun there is.”
Supermarkets need time ‘to deal with logistics’
UKSOL is hoping that more major outlets will start selling the devices soon. Moore said retailers are “very keen”, before adding: “The availability may be limited at first, so that could be frustrating for people. It may take a while.”
Specialist supplier Hampshire Generators said they expect to soon start selling a smaller plug-in solar panel kit – with a less powerful 400W microinverter – for between £350 and £450.
![](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/SEI_301776504.webp?w=644)
Managing director Andrew Williams said he expected the kit, which can be clipped onto balconies, to become ENA compliant in the coming days.
But it may take a while before supermarkets and big retailers start selling a range of plug-in kits in store. “They need to get stock together and deal with those logistics,” said Williams.
It could mean many people waiting until after winter to invest in plug-in solar, the supplier warned. “It’s a shame, because the weather is starting to change. It may have to be something that takes off in spring.”
Hemal Morjaria, chief commercial officer at City Plumbing, said the retailer would have UKSOL plug-in solar systems “available for purchase either online or in branch” on Thursday.
“Due to the size and nature of the products, these kits will not be held in store but available for home delivery,” Morjaria added.
Hopes for prices to come down
Expectations that all kinds of solar plug-in kits would be available for around £400 had been unrealistic, said experts.
“The price will vary quite a bit, depending on how much power they can generate, and whether it comes as part of a kit that is ready to mount,” said Dylan Ryan, an energy engineering expert at Edinburgh Napier University.
Solar Energy UK said it expects plug-in solar costs to come down if the devices take off in the UK like they have in Germany.
“As demand is fulfilled and supplies increase, prices would be expected to fall over time,” said Gareth Simkins, spokesperson for the trade association.
A spokesperson for ENA, which represents the UK’s energy network operators, said only a “limited number” of solar plug-in devices had become compliant so far. But compliance was “moving at pace”, they added.
A DESNZ spokesperson said: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to order this Thursday from retailers including Argos.”
The “transformative” plug-in technology “can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills”, they said. Legal changes follow rigorous safety testing which shows “compliant panels are safe and compatible with UK wiring”, they added.
summary: UK households will be able to buy compliant plug-in solar panel kits starting this Thursday following recent legal changes. British company UKSOL is the first to meet regulatory compliance, offering a 460W single-panel system for £699 and an 890W two-panel system for £999 through suppliers like Argos and City Plumbing. While delivery will be available immediately, in-store availability at major retailers and supermarkets is expected to take several weeks due to logistical challenges.
key_points: UK households can purchase compliant plug-in solar panel kits starting August 27.
UKSOL is the first company to meet Energy Networks Association compliance, pricing its kits at £699 and £999.
Kits will initially be available for delivery only, with in-store stocking at major retailers expected to take several weeks.
The government estimates that plug-in solar users can reduce their energy bills by £70 to £110 annually.

title: Even Scott Bessent can’t beat the markets
author: Matthew Lynn
content:
![Scott Bessent](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000498948612_17873224622020_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqD3d2dmOlWYuQkR76XZjLQKOylOV7i1cNNz18XOj47vE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Scott Bessent](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000498948612_17873224622020_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqD3d2dmOlWYuQkR76XZjLQKOylOV7i1cNNz18XOj47vE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
If the US president wanted a treasury secretary who could take on the markets and beat them, then Scott Bessent would be the man to choose.
It is not just that he is a former hedge-fund guy. He is a former George Soros hedge-fund guy. Big macro plays on currencies and bonds are what he does best, and he wins more often than he loses.
There is just one problem. Even a trader as skilled as Bessent can’t beat the markets for long when the facts are against him – and the harder he tries, the more badly he will get burnt.
It has been a dramatic few weeks for followers of US high finance. First, the US treasury dramatically intervened to prop up the yen. Then, at the close of last week, it stepped into the market to prevent bond yields from soaring out of control.
A rout in the bond markets has already sent 30-year yields up to levels not seen since before the 2008 financial crisis, and 10-year yields are not far behind.
With the total US national debt going past $40tn (£29.3tn) this week, well before forecasts, the cost of debt repayments is becoming punishing even for a country as rich as the US. The interest bill alone is estimated at $1.2tn this year, and as bond yields climb, it is rising all the time.
We may see more policy moves this week. “We have a big toolkit, so we’ll see,” Bessent said in an interview on Thursday. It is not hard to imagine what he had in mind.
The Treasury could buy up more bonds directly. It could try to bully the Fed, now under the control of Trump’s hand-picked chairman, Kevin Warsh, into buying more government debt, with printed money if necessary. It could try to lean on other central banks around the world to buy up more US bonds. Or it could simply try and bully the markets into submission. We will find out in the next few days. The real question, however, is whether it will work.
Perhaps. To some degree, Bessent is just doing what comes most naturally to him. As a key executive to the prominent hedge fund trader George Soros, the man who famously “broke the pound” in 1992, Bessent’s instincts are to intervene in the market. He’s good at it, and he knows when to catch traders and banks off guard.
The trouble is, clever financial tricks are not going to work. Sure, it was effective for a few hours. And yet, the yen is already back below the level where the US started to wade into the market, and it only took a few hours for bond yields to start rising again after Bessent’s first round of intervention.
The core problem is this. Governments around the world have borrowed too much for too long, and the US is guiltier than most. It took almost 200 years for the US national debt to hit $20tn, the level it reached during Donald Trump’s first term in 2016. It only took a decade for it to double all over again.
Debt as a percentage of GDP has hit 126pc, higher than both Britain and France, two countries that are regularly targeted by the bond markets for their excessive borrowing, and behind only Japan and Italy among the world’s major economies.
Perhaps most alarmingly of all, borrowing is still forecast to hit almost 6pc of GDP this year, even though there is no major economic emergency to deal with, and the growth is healthy. Ronald Reagan, the 40th US president, used to joke that “the deficit was big enough to look after itself”. Unfortunately, that is no longer true. It has turned into a serious problem
The twist is that, unlike Japan, or just about every major European economy, the US actually has the space to fix the problem. Any country that is creating companies the size of SpaceX, with a market value of $1.8tn, or Anthropic, with an expected market value when it goes public later this year of at least $1.5tn, is still creating wealth on a formidable scale.
Employment is strong, wages are high, and the corporate sector is raking in record profits. The various branches of the US state only collect 27pc of GDP in tax, and the federal government only 18pc, compared to 36pc in Britain and 45pc in France.
There is plenty of scope to raise taxes modestly – indeed, the tariffs, for all the criticism they attracted, were a start – and simply holding spending at its current level while the economy grows at 3pc a year should take care of the problem very quickly.
And yet, there has not been a president with any serious commitment to balancing the books since Bill Clinton back in the 1990s. Joe Biden borrowed wildly and wasted most of the money on industrial subsidies, while Trump’s second term has been dominated by tax cuts and expensive foreign wars, instead of the sustained assault on spending that he promised on the campaign trail.
Bessent can play all the tricks he learnt running one of the world’s most ruthlessly successful hedge funds as much as he likes. He can try to bully the markets into submission or find a whole series of clever ways of stopping yields from running out of control. It is not going to work.
Until there is a president who is willing to modestly raise taxes and hold spending until the deficit starts to come under control, and, even better, who sets out a two-term plan to balance the books, the chaos is only going to continue – and not even the most skilful of treasury secretaries will be able to control the markets for long.
summary: Despite Scott Bessent's background as a skilled hedge-fund trader capable of market interventions, even he cannot permanently defeat the markets when economic fundamentals are unfavourable. The US faces a severe debt crisis with national debt surpassing $40 trillion, soaring bond yields, and heavy borrowing despite healthy economic growth. Although the US possesses the economic wealth and tax policy space to resolve the problem, the ongoing market chaos will persist until political leadership commits to modest tax increases and spending restraint.
key_points: US Treasury interventions to prop up the yen and control soaring bond yields have only provided temporary relief.
US national debt has exceeded $40 trillion, with debt as a percentage of GDP reaching 126pc.
Borrowing is forecast to hit nearly 6pc of GDP this year despite healthy economic growth and strong employment.
The US has the capacity to fix the debt through modest tax increases and spending controls, but lacks presidential commitment to balance the budget.

title: The blueprint for Burnham’s plan to ‘rewire Britain’ could be found 700 miles away
author: Dan Haygarth
content:
Andy Burnham thinks Britain’s political culture is broken.
While his first few weeks in Downing Street have focused on grassroots policy, the new prime minister has made no secret of his plan to make his premiership a “circuit breaker” for Britain, starting with the “biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen”.
The former Greater Manchester mayor wants to bring about the “end of neoliberalism” and move beyond “trickle-down economics”, rooting decision-making and power in communities, rather than centrally in London.
He said that his administration would follow a “Makerfield test”, making decisions based on whether they would improve the lives of people in constituencies like his – a brand of politics driven by lifting up those he believes have been forgotten for decades.
No 10 North, announced to much fanfare last month, is just the start of Mr Burnham’s devolution revolution. He wants far more power transferred from Westminster to local leaders and has already unveiled plans to give all mayors of England’s city regions a share of income tax revenue for the first time.
This, combined with a plan to retake public control of essential services, is the key plank in the business-friendly socialist policy agenda Mr Burnham has dubbed “Manchesterism”. But to find an example of how Manchesterism could succeed, you may have to look a little further afield.
Found around 700 miles from the prime minister’s former patch, on the Nervión river that runs through Northern Spain’s Basque Country to the Bay of Biscay, Bilbao was historically a thriving port city that became a hive of heavy industry in the 20th century.
But like many port cities around the United Kingdom, it suffered the harsh impacts of deindustrialisation in the years after the Second World War, hitting a nadir in the 1980s as shipyard and factory closures caused large-scale unemployment.
“During the Eighties, because we were in a quite similar situation as Liverpool and other places in England,” Ivan Jiménez, president of the Port of Bilbao, tells The Independent.
![Ivan Jiminez, president of the Port of Bilbao](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/12/14/37/IVAN-JIMENEZ-AIRA-credit-Port-of-Bilbao-5.jpg)
“People used to say, ‘No opportunities, this is dead, the steel industry has died.’
“Here, in the Eighties, I remember that we here had a 25 per cent unemployment rate. It was devastated.”
But the Bilbao of 2026 has come a long way since the 1980s, and its recovery will be of particular interest to the UK’s new prime minister.
Once home to the city’s maritime might, the banks of the river are now most notable for the Guggenheim museum, built in 1997 to become the ship-shaped symbol of its revival.
Between its opening and 2015, GDP in the city more than doubled as it pivoted from a declining steel and shipbuilding economy to become a hub of clean energy, advanced manufacturing and biotechnology, with tourism and culture becoming key economies.
From 2000 to 2018, the city had the highest level of economic growth in Spain and, according to Mr Jiménez, that owes a lot to its devolved powers, similar to those Mr Burnham wishes to introduce in the UK.
Bilbao’s province, Biscay, is one of three which make up the autonomous community of the Basque Country, a region marked by a prominent separatist movement, part of which desires complete independence from Spain.
But the Basque Country’s self-governance means it has sweeping powers over tax, education, health, economic strategy and welfare.
As such, residents do not pay state income tax.
Instead of being funded by the Spanish central government in Madrid, Bilbao collects 100 per cent of its own income tax through its three provinces and keeps the majority, sending a fixed annual quota to the capital to pay for national services, such as the military.
![Bilbao has seen a significant transformation in recent years](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/13/14/48/AdobeStock_1732780383.jpg)
Mr Burnham hopes that a similarly less centralised approach would revive the fortunes of Britain’s post-industrial regions. Ensuring that money and power are not concentrated in London is central to his agenda.
And, like in Bilbao, taxation could be key to that.
Last month, the prime minister announced that mayors in England will get to keep a share of taxes collected in their regions to “bring power home” to communities.
The regional leaders will receive a share of income tax revenues for the first time under the plans, which the government has described as the “biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”, and would bolster their funding – on top of settlements currently allocated by central government.
Such autonomy has helped Bilbao thrive; according to Mr Jiménez, it proves that “you can manage without the dependency from the central state”.
“At the end, about 90 per cent of the taxes that are collected in the Basque Country stay in the Basque Country.
“With this autonomy, and in collaboration also with different other institutions – also from the state, also from Europe – they transformed a city that was based on heavy industry to advanced services and new industries.”
Mr Jiménez believes that consistent public investment through locally collected income taxes has allowed the region to develop in a way that suits itself, rather than having a path chosen for it by central government.
But this has been boosted, he says, by tailored private investment and collaboration with the public sector, such as the public-private partnership Bilbao Ría 2000, tasked with regenerating post-industrial sites.
![The distinctive Guggenheim museum helped transform Bilbao’s fortunes](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/13/14/58/AdobeStock_496775206.jpg)
“Collaboration is quite easy here,” Mr Jiménez says. To have a meeting here with any kind of politician for an entrepreneur, it’s quite easy.
“They used to tell us, for example, you go to Madrid or other places to have a meeting with the regional ministry, it’s quite difficult.
“In our case, the doors are always open because we are looking all the time for investment, research, development.”
It is, in many ways, redolent of what the MP for Makerfield wishes to achieve with his flagship policy of Number 10 North. Rather than everything being delivered through a nation’s capital, he hopes his new Manchester outpost will mean meetings for investment do not have to take place centrally.
Where Mr Burnham may struggle, however, is installing such a devolved economic system from scratch, Mr Jiménez says.
It is not a case of one size fits all, he believes, and such plans have to be bespoke in each region.
Though the English mayors have powers over matters such as transport and in their combined authorities, giving them control of taxes represents a radical change to the system.
And for Mr Jiménez, the reason it works in the Basque Country is its historic autonomy.
“If you ask me, nowadays, could it be possible to create this from zero in the Spanish state? I would find it very, very difficult,” he explains.
“If you want to translate this to any other place, and if you don't have a culture – a culture in our case coming from history – it could be a very difficult talk or discussion.
“That’s very clear, and would probably be much easier to implement this in a place where this identity plays a main role.”
Strong identity and pride – whether it is national in the case of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland or regional in places like the Liverpool City Region (where a ‘Scouse not English’ attitude exists) – and ensuring people believe that their part of the UK can thrive is key to making it work.
Mr Jiménez added: “You say: ‘I may feel English or not English, but I’m very linked to my region, and even if I feel English 100 per cent, I want to promote, I want to stay here, I want my children and grandchildren to grow up here with a lot of opportunities.’”
Retaining talent in the Basque Country is the job of Amaia Jugo, managing director of Bizkaia Talent.
![Amaia Jugo, managing director of Bizkaia Talent](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/13/14/42/Amaia-Jugo.jpg)
When opening No 10 North, the prime minister recalled his own experience of moving to London as a graduate in the early 1990s to find work, as he promised to make that a thing of the past.
To allow people to build their lives in their home towns and cities, he has also pledged a project of reindustrialisation, not dissimilar to that in the Basque Country, bringing a green energy revolution to areas which lost their core industries in the 20th century.
About how the Basque Country has done so and prevents a brain drain, Ms Jugo said: “We explain that we have very good opportunities in strategic industries. We have different clusters, like automation, where you can have very good opportunities.
“When young people finish university, they are usually looking at London or Madrid. It is very important to be connected with them to show that they will have good opportunities here and can do a very good job in companies that have a good impact in our ecosystem.
“We have to change. We know that some industries are going to disappear or become smaller. So we have to understand that we need different industries.”
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is pursuing a devolution revolution aimed at moving power away from London, giving local leaders a share of income tax revenue, and reviving post-industrial communities. To find a potential blueprint for this approach, the article looks to Bilbao in Spain's Basque Country, which successfully transformed its economy after deindustrialisation thanks to sweeping self-governance and tax autonomy. While Burnham hopes to replicate this success in the UK, experts note that implementing such a system from scratch without historic regional autonomy could prove challenging.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham's "Manchesterism" agenda seeks to decentralize power from London and give English city region mayors a share of income tax revenue.
Bilbao in Spain's Basque Country successfully transitioned from heavy industry to clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and tourism following severe deindustrialisation in the 1980s.

The Basque Country retains the vast majority of its locally collected income tax through its historic autonomy, funding its own services rather than depending heavily on the central government in Madrid.

Local leaders note that while Bilbao's model relies on strong historic self-governance and public-private collaboration, establishing a similar decentralized tax system from scratch in the UK could be difficult.

title: Five passengers injured after laptop catches fire mid-flight
author: Lily Shanagher
content:
A laptop burst into flames on an American Airlines plane in mid-flight, leaving five passengers with burns.
One person required medical treatment after a passenger’s laptop caught fire on the flight, which was carrying 133 passengers from Atlanta, Georgia, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas on Friday.
The pilot reported the incident to air traffic control, telling staff there was a “cabin fire in the back of the airplane” and that flight attendants were trying to put it out, according to audio obtained by CBS News.
The pilot told air traffic control: “I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop. The laptop is contained about mid-aircraft.”
As cabin crew members worked to control the fire, the plane continued to approach the airport and made a safe landing. Emergency workers were waiting on the ground.
The airline told the BBC that the flight had landed safely “after reports of smoke from a customer’s device during landing”, adding: “We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device.”
summary: A passenger's laptop caught fire mid-flight on an American Airlines plane traveling from Atlanta to Dallas Fort Worth, resulting in burns for five passengers. The pilot reported the cabin fire to air traffic control while cabin crew successfully contained the device. The aircraft landed safely with emergency responders waiting on the ground.
key_points: A laptop caught fire on an American Airlines flight carrying 133 passengers from Atlanta to Dallas Fort Worth.
Five passengers sustained burns during the incident.
The pilot reported a cabin fire to air traffic control while flight attendants worked to extinguish it.
The plane landed safely and was met by emergency workers on the ground.

title: Usain Bolt’s 100m record broken at World Humanoid Robot Games
author: Reuters
content:
![Staff members prepare Booster Robotics humanoid robots before the opening ceremony for the second World Humanoid Robot Games](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-22T110026Z_1489010015_RC2M3NAU6SAR_RTRMADP_3_CHINA-TECH-ROBOT-GAMES-1787396749.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
A humanoid robot developed by Chinese smartphone maker Honor ran 100 metres (328ft) in 9.32 seconds, China’s state broadcaster has reported, beating the human world record held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.
The robot, dubbed Lightning, reached a peak speed of 14.5 metres (47.6ft) per second during a preparatory test event for the second World Humanoid Robot Games, which opened in Beijing on Saturday.
